paragraphs: Diffusion models trained on separate portions of a dataset can produce remarkably similar images when started from the same noise. This paper investigates how much of that agreement follows from shared statistical structure. Its central explanation is a linear effect: Gaussian statistics common to the training splits already account for much of the generated output.

The authors develop a random matrix theory analysis of how finite training data affect a linear denoiser and its sampling process. Limited data effectively change the noise level, causing excessive shrinkage along directions with little variation and drawing samples toward the dataset mean. Their variance analysis separates disagreement into differences across data directions, differences across inputs, and dependence on dataset size.

The framework also analyzes complete sampling trajectories. It closely predicts linear diffusion behavior, and the authors validate predictions on UNet and DiT models in a regime without memorization. These results provide a principled baseline for understanding reproducibility: some agreement across training splits can arise from shared data statistics, while their spectral structure helps explain where outputs diverge.
icml-2026-a-random-matrix-theory-perspec.tldr: A random matrix analysis explains much cross-split diffusion consistency through shared Gaussian statistics and predicts how finite data affect generated outputs.

paragraphs: Long-tailed recognition asks a model to recognize classes with very different amounts of training data. The paper attributes an important difficulty to optimizer blindness: accumulated gradient magnitude can be confused with how much semantic information a class lacks. Corrections based on fixed class frequencies do not track the changing state of supervision or individual parameter updates.

AES addresses this problem at three stages. Adaptive Residual Supervision adjusts supervision through a mechanism called precision shielding, intended to assess its completeness during training. Entropy-aware PCGrad uses gradient entropy to quantify task specificity and resolve conflicts between parameter updates. At inference, Sample-level Conflict Arbitrated Fusion routes predictions according to the difficulty of each individual example.

Together, these components make correction depend on the model’s current state and the sample being processed. Experiments on CIFAR-100-LT, ImageNet-LT, and iNaturalist 2018 report state-of-the-art performance. The stated result is a better balance between maintaining reliable recognition of common classes and distinguishing rare classes, linking improvements to coordinated adjustments across supervision, optimization, and prediction.
icml-2026-aes-curing-optimizer-blindness.tldr: AES adjusts supervision, gradient conflict handling, and prediction routing dynamically to improve recognition of both common and rare classes.

paragraphs: Models that process vision, audio, and language need evaluations that establish how well they combine these inputs. AVI-Bench addresses a gap in systematic testing of audio-visual intelligence. Its tasks require joint interpretation of sound and visual information, making their interaction central to the evaluation rather than merely including both kinds of input.

The benchmark organizes evaluation around three cognitively inspired stages: perception, understanding, and reasoning. This structure supports more detailed diagnosis of capabilities and failure modes than a single overall assessment. An extension, AVI-Bench-PriSe, uses unfamiliar stimuli with little semantic content to probe primitive audio-visual sensation and assess generalization beyond familiar training distributions.

Experiments with open-source and closed-source models reveal substantial limitations in current systems. Drawing on these findings, the authors introduce a four-level taxonomy of audio-visual intelligence. The contribution is an evaluation framework that connects different kinds of cross-modal ability with tests of unfamiliar inputs, helping distinguish successful performance in familiar settings from broader audio-visual generalization.
icml-2026-avi-bench-toward-human-like-au.tldr: AVI-Bench tests joint audio-visual perception, understanding, and reasoning, revealing substantial limitations in current multimodal models.

paragraphs: Spending more computation at inference can improve reasoning from a fixed language model, but the sampling procedure determines whether that improvement is practical. Sequential Metropolis Hastings sampling is difficult to parallelize and can produce very long waits. The paper reports a 95th-percentile latency of 1,318 seconds on MATH500 at a 128× budget for this approach.

Adaptive Sequential Monte Carlo maintains parallel candidate trajectories, called particles, and adjusts their population to problem hardness. Its cache coherent resampling mechanism makes this practical for Transformers. When particles inherit previous trajectories, the system rearranges their key-value caches and associated tensors, preserving already computed prefixes instead of calculating them again.

At the same MATH500 budget, the method achieves 80.6% exact-match accuracy with a 95th-percentile latency of 73.7 seconds. It also offers high-accuracy settings beyond where best-of-n sampling saturates. The analysis finds that severe particle collapse strongly predicts failures, while changing the resampling scheme has limited influence. This connects useful reasoning gains to both efficient execution and the health of the particle population.
icml-2026-cache-coherent-resampling-for-.tldr: Parallel adaptive sampling with cache reuse substantially reduces reasoning tail latency while supporting high-accuracy inference from a fixed language model.

paragraphs: Scientific spectra contain structured physical information, and their predictions must respect constraints such as conservation laws and characteristic spectral geometry. The paper argues that treating spectra as unconstrained sequences overlooks this structure. That matters for materials discovery, where an accurate prediction should also remain compatible with the physics represented by the spectrum.

DeepSciReasoner combines two parts: a decoder designed around spectral structure and a physical reasoning process that preserves constraints. Electronic density of states serves as the main motivating example. The approach aims to retain detailed spectral information while enforcing the physical conditions that govern it, making those conditions part of prediction rather than a separate consideration.

The authors evaluate the framework on electronic and phonon density of states, X-ray absorption near-edge structure, and Raman spectra. They report substantial gains in predictive accuracy while maintaining physical consistency across these tasks. The findings support the framework’s proposed reuse across different scientific spectra: structure-aware decoding and constraint-preserving reasoning can work together within a shared prediction paradigm.
icml-2026-deep-scientific-reasoning-unde.tldr: DeepSciReasoner improves scientific spectrum prediction by combining structure-aware decoding with reasoning that preserves physical constraints.

paragraphs: Unlearnable examples contain visually imperceptible changes intended to undermine models trained on them. Their effectiveness depends on whether those changes remain disruptive when training defenses are applied. The paper argues that existing methods often lose robustness because they rely on heuristic designs or restrict perturbations to a narrow domain.

DUNE optimizes two perturbation branches separately, one in the spatial domain and one in the color domain. It links these perturbations to labels induced by shifts, encouraging a model to learn features tied to the perturbations that generalize poorly. Expanding the perturbation domain is intended to strengthen the disruptive signal. An additional ensemble strategy brings diverse pretrained models into the optimization to further improve unlearnability.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet compare DUNE with 12 state-of-the-art schemes under seven mainstream defenses. The authors report stronger robustness and lower average test accuracies, with reported values ranging from 14.95% to 50.82%. Here, lower accuracy is the desired outcome: it indicates that training on the perturbed examples leaves the resulting model less able to generalize.
icml-2026-dual-branch-robust-unlearnable.tldr: DUNE combines spatial and color perturbations with model ensembling to make unlearnable examples more robust against training defenses.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks face a tension between theoretical expressivity and practical performance. Some efficient models capture particular graph properties well but lack general expressivity guarantees. Models with universal expressivity can instead be expensive or generalize poorly. This paper introduces Equivariant Noise GNNs to bring these capabilities together within a practical framework.

ENGNNs add random noise features while enforcing a structured response to transformations of that noise, including nodewise orthogonal transformations. This equivariance makes the treatment of randomness part of the architecture’s design. The authors prove that the property reduces theoretical sample complexity, providing a reason that noise can improve expressivity without imposing the same generalization burden as less structured uses.

The framework achieves theoretical universal expressivity and retains the practical linear scalability of standard message-passing networks. Experiments cover prediction at the node, link, subgraph, and whole-graph levels, with performance comparable to more computationally expensive expressive models. The contribution therefore connects a theoretical generalization result with a broadly evaluated design for using randomness efficiently in graph learning.
icml-2026-expressive-graph-neural-networ.tldr: ENGNNs use noise equivariantly to combine universal graph expressivity, reduced theoretical sample complexity, and practical message-passing scalability.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization when the only available feedback says which of two candidate points has the larger objective value. The algorithm cannot directly request function values or derivatives. Its goal is to find an approximately stationary point of a non-convex function, meaning a point where the gradient is small, without claiming to find a global optimum.

For twice-differentiable functions with Lipschitz-continuous gradients and Hessians, the authors develop a classical algorithm requiring roughly n²/ε^1.5 comparison queries, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here n is the dimension and ε controls stationarity accuracy. A central subroutine estimates the normalized Hessian to accuracy δ using roughly n² log(1/δ) queries, again suppressing additional logarithmic factors.

The paper also considers a quantum comparison oracle that permits queries in superposition. In that model, its quantum algorithm uses roughly n/ε^1.5 queries. The result improves the dimension dependence of query complexity from quadratic to linear under the stated oracle model, showing how much optimization information comparisons can provide under these smoothness assumptions.
icml-2026-finding-stationary-points-by-c.tldr: Under smoothness assumptions, comparison-only algorithms find approximately stationary points with quadratic classical or linear quantum dependence on dimension.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning on benign examples can weaken a language model’s previously learned safety behavior. This paper examines how that degradation develops during training. It focuses on the evolving parameter trajectory, extending analyses that compare only the parameters or hidden states before and after fine-tuning and therefore overlook the intervening dynamics.

The authors identify cumulative movement toward parameter directions associated with dangerous behavior as a mechanism underlying safety loss. They use this finding to develop Sample-Level Quantification of Safety Degradation, or SQSD. The method assigns each training example a continuous risk score by measuring how its induced parameter update aligns with safety and danger directions. Risk therefore reflects training influence rather than simply whether an example appears harmful.

Across three models and two datasets, SQSD separates high-risk and low-risk examples better than the compared baselines, and its scores consistently predict degradation severity. The authors also report strong transfer across architectures, model sizes, and parameter-efficient methods. These findings support sample-level analysis as a way to identify potentially damaging contributions within otherwise benign fine-tuning data.
icml-2026-from-parameter-dynamics-to-ris.tldr: SQSD scores fine-tuning examples by their parameter-update directions to predict how strongly they may degrade a language model’s safety.

paragraphs: Producing an exam drawing requires a model to understand a question, reason about its requirements, and express the answer visually. GenExam evaluates this combination. The paper identifies a gap between exam benchmarks focused on understanding and reasoning and generation benchmarks focused on depicting knowledge or visual concepts, leaving rigorous drawing examinations comparatively neglected.

The benchmark contains 1,000 examples across 10 subjects, with exam-style prompts organized into a four-level taxonomy. Each problem includes reference images and detailed scoring points. These support evaluation of both semantic correctness and visual plausibility, so the assessment considers whether an image communicates the required answer as well as whether its visual presentation makes sense.

Tests of 17 text-to-image and unified models show that GenExam is challenging. Open-source models consistently trail the leading closed-source systems in these experiments. The benchmark’s contribution is to make integrated understanding, reasoning, and generation the object of assessment, using explicit scoring criteria to examine image generation as a substantive answer to an academic problem.
icml-2026-genexam-a-multidisciplinary-te.tldr: GenExam evaluates image generation through 1,000 multidisciplinary exam problems that require integrated understanding, reasoning, and drawing.

paragraphs: Compressing language-model weights to two bits creates a difficult representation and optimization problem. Scalar quantization is easy to optimize but can severely reduce performance at this precision. Vector quantization offers greater representational capacity, yet selecting discrete entries from a codebook obstructs straightforward end-to-end training. LC-QAT aims to combine useful properties of both approaches.

The framework represents quantized weights through a learned affine mapping over discrete vectors. This supplies a strong post-training quantization initialization and allows fully differentiable optimization without an explicit codebook lookup during the training forward pass. Its two-bit setting applies to weights. The paper connects its data efficiency to the quality of the starting quantized model.

Across diverse language models, LC-QAT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art quantization-aware training methods while using only 0.1%–10% of their training data. These findings suggest that improving the quantized representation and its initialization can substantially reduce the data needed for subsequent training. The contribution is a trainable vector-quantization framework aimed at practical deployment under extreme weight compression.
icml-2026-lc-qat-data-efficient-2-bit-qa.tldr: LC-QAT enables differentiable two-bit weight quantization and outperforms compared QAT methods using a small fraction of their training data.

paragraphs: The paper asks how many embedding dimensions are needed to represent every possible retrieval target containing at most k objects from a collection of m. It defines the minimal embeddable dimension as the smallest dimension admitting such an object-vector configuration. For inner product, Euclidean distance, and cosine similarity, this dimension grows proportionally to k, independently of collection size.

Exact retrieval capacity differs from retrieval with a protective score margin. The authors therefore study a robust version requiring unit-length vectors and a gap ε between scores. They derive a collection-size-dependent ceiling on feasible margins, approaching 1/√k when m is much larger than k. A Gaussian centroid construction supplies an upper bound in the feasible-margin regime.

Synthetic top-two simulations support the theoretical claims. On LIMIT and LIMIT-small, simple embedding retrieval baselines can overfit and exceed the reported single-vector LLM embedding baseline. Together, these results rule out insufficient exact geometric capacity as the obstruction considered here. The robustness analysis separately shows why demanding score separation introduces constraints absent from exact representability alone.
icml-2026-mathbbr-2k-is-theoretically-la.tldr: Exact top-k retrieval needs only dimension proportional to k, while robust retrieval with score margins faces additional feasibility constraints.

paragraphs: Memory helps language-model agents handle complex tasks, but it also creates material that attackers may try to extract. MemPot defends these memory systems by inserting optimized honeypots: trap documents designed to be retrieved by attackers while remaining inconspicuous during benign use. The defense uses interactions with these documents as evidence for detecting extraction attempts.

A two-stage optimization process shapes the trap documents toward those competing goals. The authors model detection using Wald’s Sequential Probability Ratio Test, which accumulates evidence across sampling rounds. Under this formulation, they prove that MemPot requires fewer sampling rounds on average than optimal static detectors, connecting the defense design to an explicit sequential detection result.

Experiments report a 50% improvement in detection AUROC and an 80% increase in true positive rate under low false positive rate constraints. The authors also report zero online inference latency and preserved agent utility on standard tasks. These findings support the proposed combination of selective trap retrieval and sequential detection as an effective defense in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-mempot-defending-against-memor.tldr: MemPot uses optimized memory honeypots and sequential evidence gathering to detect extraction attacks while preserving tested agent utility.

paragraphs: MVISTA-4D addresses robotic manipulation by predicting how a three-dimensional scene develops over time. Starting from one RGBD observation, containing color and depth, the model generates additional viewpoints. These can be projected back into three-dimensional space and fused into a more complete evolving scene, giving the robot a richer imagined future.

The model explicitly combines features across viewpoints and across color and depth. This encourages agreement between modalities and geometric alignment between views. Turning an imagined future into executable actions introduces another challenge: multiple actions can explain the same transition, so directly inferring actions from that transition is an ambiguous problem.

The authors address this ambiguity by optimizing a trajectory-level latent representation at test time through the generative model. A residual inverse dynamics model then converts that trajectory prior into executable actions. Experiments across three datasets and platforms report strong results for both scene generation and manipulation. The work connects consistent multi-view prediction with an action-inference procedure designed to use the generated future across an entire trajectory.
icml-2026-mvista-4d-view-consistent-4d-w.tldr: MVISTA-4D generates geometrically consistent evolving scenes from one RGBD view and uses test-time trajectory optimization to infer robot actions.

paragraphs: Probabilistic robustness evaluates a model under input perturbations drawn from a distribution. Its usefulness depends on how well that distribution represents the disturbances being considered. The paper targets a weakness in existing formulations: assuming the perturbation distribution is fixed and known, even when that knowledge is unavailable in practice.

Non-parametric probabilistic robustness learns an optimized perturbation distribution from data rather than requiring one to be specified beforehand. The aim is a conservative assessment under distributional uncertainty. The authors develop an estimator using a Gaussian mixture model, accommodating both input-dependent and input-independent perturbations, and provide theoretical relationships between adversarial robustness, ordinary probabilistic robustness, and their proposed metric.

Experiments span CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet, using ResNet18/50, WideResNet50, and VGG16. The resulting robustness estimates are lower than estimates based on commonly assumed perturbation distributions. This is the intended conservative behavior: evaluation becomes less optimistic when the disturbance model is learned for that purpose, making the choice of perturbation distribution an explicit part of robustness assessment.
icml-2026-non-parametric-probabilistic-r.tldr: NPPR learns perturbation distributions from data to produce more conservative probabilistic robustness estimates under distributional uncertainty.

paragraphs: Many fMRI foundation models first group brain measurements into predefined regions using an atlas. That representation can discard information from individual voxels and introduce biases tied to the chosen atlas. Omni-fMRI instead learns directly from voxel-level signals, making fine-grained measurements the basis of its representation without requiring predefined regional divisions.

Working at voxel resolution raises computational demands. The model introduces dynamic patching to reduce those costs while preserving informative spatial structure. This enables self-supervised pretraining on 49,497 fMRI sessions from nine datasets. The contribution combines an atlas-free representation with a mechanism intended to make training at that resolution scalable.

The authors also establish a benchmark covering 11 datasets and a range of resting-state and task-based fMRI tasks. This provides a shared basis for reproducibility and comparison. Across the reported experiments, Omni-fMRI consistently outperforms existing foundation models. The findings support direct voxel-level learning as a useful alternative to atlas-based representations, with the benchmark providing a framework for evaluating that approach across different fMRI tasks.
icml-2026-omni-fmri-a-universal-atlas-fr.tldr: Omni-fMRI uses dynamic patching to learn directly from voxel-level brain signals and outperforms existing foundation models in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Models that handle streaming video, audio, and text can face high computational costs as input grows. Token compression reduces the amount of information processed, but uniform retention rules overlook differences between layers. The paper also argues that compression driven by a single modality can miss the importance of alignment across modalities.

OmniFit is a training-free framework that separates profiling of these interactions from inference execution. Its Layer-Adaptive Heterogeneity Profiling allocates computational budgets according to each layer’s redundancy and modality preferences. Alignment-Rectified Token Selection then identifies tokens that align semantically with cues from other modalities, so compression considers relationships between inputs as well as layer-specific needs.

Across three model series and 10 benchmarks, the authors report retaining 98% of model performance with 20% token usage. They also report up to 2.31× end-to-end inference speedup and 2.5× VRAM savings. These results support the value of allocating compression unevenly and preserving cross-modal connections, producing a stronger measured trade-off between performance and computational resources than the compared methods.
icml-2026-omnifit-bridging-modalities-vi.tldr: OmniFit compresses tokens according to layer needs and cross-modal alignment, retaining 98% of reported performance with 20% token usage.

paragraphs: When observational information cannot determine a single causal answer, partial identification aims to provide informative bounds. Optimal transport can help construct these bounds, but its computational and statistical demands grow difficult when both potential outcomes and confounders are high-dimensional. Reducing dimension helps with tractability, yet can discard information relevant to the bounds.

The proposed estimator divides transport into a low-dimensional signal component and a high-dimensional residual component. It retains the residual contribution by estimating its transport energy with Sliced Wasserstein distance. This addresses the information loss of projection-only approaches while keeping the high-dimensional part computationally manageable. The authors also provide a data-driven rule for choosing the signal dimension.

The theory gives conditions linking the approximation gap to the structure of the residual component. Empirically, the method consistently improves on projection-only baselines by recovering transport energy those methods lose. The result is more informative causal bounds with tractable computation in high dimensions, showing why retaining an estimate of residual information can matter even after identifying a compact signal representation.
icml-2026-partial-identification-under-h.tldr: A signal-and-residual transport estimator improves high-dimensional causal bounds by recovering information discarded by projection-only methods.

paragraphs: LoRA represents a trainable weight update as the product of two smaller matrices. Many different pairs of factors can represent exactly the same update. This paper shows that applying differentially private stochastic gradient descent directly to those factors makes the resulting noise depend on that arbitrary representation, with potentially unbounded amplification in the actual weight update.

PRISM builds privacy protection around the intrinsic update geometry. Its mechanism is gauge invariant, meaning equivalent factorizations do not change the relevant perturbation behavior. It avoids bilinear noise amplification and supports an efficient low-dimensional noise sampler. The authors also derive a closed-form description of the effective noise introduced into the update matrix.

The paper establishes standard epsilon-delta differential privacy guarantees and bounded, representation-independent perturbations. It further introduces an adaptive update rule designed to prevent optimization from amplifying injected privacy noise, improving numerical stability in practice. These contributions connect privacy guarantees to the geometry of low-rank adaptation, addressing a source of instability that arises even when the represented model update is unchanged.
icml-2026-prism-gauge-invariant-tangent-.tldr: PRISM provides differentially private LoRA updates whose noise is invariant to equivalent factorizations and avoids unbounded amplification.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can improve flow-based image generators, but the paper identifies two weaknesses in current training pipelines. Collapsed generation diversity wastes samples, and prompt overfitting makes models depend on particular training phrasings. A model may consequently perform poorly when the same meaning is expressed through a different paraphrase.

PromptRL places a trainable language-model prompt refiner inside the reinforcement learning loop. Training produces both a learned prompt rewriter and a coupled optimization process for image generation. This makes prompt refinement part of how the generator learns, addressing the role of wording within the training process itself.

The authors report scores of 0.97 on GenEval, 0.98 OCR accuracy, and 24.05 PickScore. For instructional editing, FLUX.1-Kontext improves from 1.19 to 1.43 EditReward with 0.06 million rollouts, surpassing the reported Gemini 2.5 Flash Image score and approximately matching ReasonEdit-Think. Across their experiments, PromptRL reaches higher performance ceilings with about 50% fewer rollouts than naive flow-only reinforcement learning, supporting joint prompt refinement as a route to more efficient post-training.
icml-2026-promptrl-prompt-matters-in-rl-.tldr: PromptRL trains prompt refinement inside the image-generation reinforcement learning loop, improving reported performance with approximately half as many rollouts.

paragraphs: Relational databases are widespread, but useful training collections are often private, scarce, and structurally diverse. This makes the large-scale pretraining strategy used for text and vision difficult to reproduce. RDB-PFN addresses that obstacle by learning entirely from synthetic data, with a generator designed to create diverse relational databases from scratch.

The approach builds on Prior-Data Fitted Networks, which learn from synthetic tasks generated using structural causal models. The authors extend this idea beyond individual tables through a Relational Prior Generator. Pretraining covers more than two million single-table and relational tasks. The resulting model adapts through in-context learning, using supplied examples from a new database to guide predictions.

On 19 real-world relational prediction tasks, RDB-PFN shows strong few-shot performance and outperforms state-of-the-art tabular foundation models evaluated on the same DFS-linearized inputs. It also uses a lightweight architecture with fast inference. These results support synthetic relational structure as a useful source of pretraining experience, demonstrating transfer from generated tasks to prediction problems in real databases.
icml-2026-relational-in-context-learning.tldr: RDB-PFN learns from synthetic relational tasks and transfers through in-context learning to strong few-shot prediction on real databases.

paragraphs: Language-model embeddings make observational text usable for treatment-effect estimation, but their high dimensionality complicates causal representation learning. In particular, empirical Wasserstein matching becomes statistically difficult enough that standard generalization guarantees can be effectively uninformative. SPIKED-CFR addresses this problem through an explicit assumption about where treatment selection bias appears.

Its spiked-structure assumption says that the discrepancy between treated and control representations lies primarily in a low-dimensional subspace. Wasserstein Projection Pursuit adversarially learns an orthogonal projection to identify and balance that discrepancy while preserving information useful for predicting outcomes. This focuses matching on the assumed bias-bearing directions within the larger semantic representation.

Under the stated structure, the authors show that discrepancy estimation depends on intrinsic dimension k rather than the full embedding dimension D. They also derive a tighter PEHE generalization bound, concerning error in heterogeneous treatment-effect estimation. Experiments on four semi-synthetic and four real-world clinical benchmarks report improved accuracy and robustness over strong baselines. The theoretical benefit therefore depends on the spiked assumption, with empirical results supporting the proposed approach.
icml-2026-spiked-cfr-causal-representati.tldr: SPIKED-CFR improves causal learning from text embeddings by balancing a low-dimensional bias subspace under an explicit spiked-structure assumption.

paragraphs: Choosing a sequence of interventions requires accounting for how a system changes over time and how decisions move it toward a desired outcome. This paper studies learning such policies from observational data. Its focus is adaptive online use, where a policy must respond as events unfold after being learned from offline records.

GIFT learns a policy conditioned on the target outcome. It rescales rewards using clipped importance weights to guide learning toward that target while stabilizing training. Clipping is central to this balance: the method uses bounded weights, and the analysis explicitly accounts for the bias introduced by clipping and approximation.

Under standard assumptions, the authors prove that the induced operator has a unique fixed point and that their procedure converges to it. They also bound the discrepancy from the policy’s true value. Experiments report significant improvements over existing methods for producing goal-conditioned policies intended for online deployment. The work thus combines an adaptive intervention objective with conditional convergence guarantees and an analysis of the approximation trade-offs involved.
icml-2026-target-driven-policy-optimizat.tldr: GIFT learns target-conditioned intervention policies from observational data using clipped importance weighting, with convergence guarantees under standard assumptions.

paragraphs: Sequential knowledge editing updates facts in a language model without retraining it from scratch. Existing approaches often add specialized constraints or regularization to keep successive edits stable. This paper investigates which mechanisms are responsible for that stability, asking whether the complexity of those additional controls is necessary for reliable updates.

The authors begin with an optimization analysis of AlphaEdit and establish a formal equivalence between one-time and sequential editing. They then extend the equivalence to a broader class of editing objectives. Their central finding is that properly accounting for accumulated editing constraints can produce stability, without requiring the specialized regularization or null-space operations used in some methods.

Experiments confirm that many commonly used regularization strategies are unnecessary for reliable sequential updates in the studied settings. The framework also extends to conflicting edits, supporting consistent behavior when updates contradict one another. The contribution provides a clearer account of why sequential editing works and a basis for simplifying editing methods while retaining the information carried by previous constraints.
icml-2026-the-labyrinth-and-the-thread-r.tldr: The paper links stable sequential knowledge editing to accumulated constraints and shows that many specialized regularizers are unnecessary in the studied settings.

paragraphs: A language model may reject a harmful request in ordinary wording yet comply when the same intent appears in an adversarial framing. This paper aims to make alignment depend more consistently on underlying intent. Its key observation is that feedback quality differs across prompt forms: some permit verifiable answers, while open-ended responses often rely on noisy reward proxies.

A symmetric consistency penalty can close this gap in an undesirable way by worsening performance on the reliable prompts. Anchor Invariance Regularization instead uses verifiable prompts as fixed reference targets. A stop-gradient operation prevents the matching loss from moving those targets, directing its correction toward open-ended variants. AIR is an auxiliary loss combined with group-based preference optimization through groups containing different prompt forms.

Across safety, moral reasoning, and mathematics, the authors report a 12.71% improvement in in-distribution group accuracy and a 33.49% improvement in out-of-distribution consistency. The results support using trustworthy feedback to guide less reliable contexts. This offers a concrete way to strengthen consistency across adversarial framings while avoiding the specific failure mode of reducing anchor performance to obtain agreement.
icml-2026-towards-context-invariant-safe.tldr: AIR uses verifiable prompts as fixed anchors to improve alignment consistency across differently framed requests.
